title: HopSkipJumpAttack: A Query-Efficient Decision-Based Attack
authors: Jianbo Chen, Michael I. Jordan, Martin J. Wainwright
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2020 (arXiv:1904.02144)

pages.title: Estimate the gradient where it matters: at the boundary
pages.subtitle: The HopSkipJump idea in one sentence

blocks.html: HopSkipJumpAttack (HSJA) tackles the same hard-label problem as the Boundary Attack and OPT, but with a sharper geometric tool. The headline result — state-of-the-art query efficiency — comes from one disciplined idea: estimate the gradient direction of the model's decision function right at the decision boundary using Monte-Carlo sampling, then combine it with a carefully sized geometric step and a binary search that snaps you back to the boundary.

The name describes the loop. Hop: estimate the gradient direction at the boundary. Skip / Jump: leap along that direction to get closer to the original image. Then land back on the boundary so the next estimate is taken in the one place it is trustworthy. Round and round, the perturbation shrinks.

Why does this beat its predecessors? The Boundary Attack random-walks and learns one bit per query; OPT and Sign-OPT optimize a direction in a separate space. HSJA instead spends its queries buying an asymptotically unbiased estimate of the true gradient direction — the most informative thing you can extract — and only where that estimate is valid.
The whole attack is a loop: find the gradient direction at the boundary, jump along it, then hop back onto the boundary.

HSJA shares the threat model of this whole family. In the hard-label / decision-based setting the attacker may query the model with any input and observes only the final predicted label — no probabilities, no logits, no gradients. Each query reveals one bit: adversarial, or not? Performance is measured by queries-to-success: how many evaluations to reach a small perturbation norm. HSJA notably supports both $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ versions, where most rivals handle only $\ell_2$.

The crucial setup is how HSJA models the classifier. Summarize it by a decision function $S(x)$ that is positive on the adversarial side and negative on the correct side; the boundary is the surface where $S(x)=0$. The catch that defines the difficulty: we can observe only the sign of $S$ — that sign is the hard label — never its value.

blocks.tex: \phi(x) = \text{sign}\big(S(x)\big) = \begin{cases} +1 & x \text{ is adversarial} \\ -1 & x \text{ is classified as the original} \end{cases}

blocks.html: Term by term: $S(x)$ is the (unobserved) real-valued decision margin; $\text{sign}(S(x))$ is all we get back, encoded as $\phi(x)$; the boundary lives where $S$ changes sign. The attack's challenge is to recover the direction of $\nabla S$ — the way the boundary tilts — from nothing but these $\pm 1$ sign readings. That is the puzzle the next section solves.
We can only feel which side of the boundary we are on. From enough such feelings, HSJA reconstructs the way the boundary leans.

sections.title: The Three Moves: Hop, Skip, Jump

pages.title: Monte-Carlo gradient-direction estimation
pages.subtitle: Reading the boundary's tilt from sign votes

blocks.html: You are standing on a point $x_t$ that sits exactly on the decision boundary. You want to know which way the boundary tilts — the direction of $\nabla S(x_t)$ — but you can only ask yes/no label questions. The trick: fire many small random probes around you, ask the oracle which side each landed on, and let the answers vote. Probes that land on the adversarial side pull the estimate one way; probes that land on the correct side pull it the other. The weighted average points along the boundary's normal.

blocks.tex: \widehat{\nabla S}(x_t) \approx \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} \phi(x_t + \delta\, u_b)\, u_b, \qquad u_b \sim \text{Uniform on unit sphere}

blocks.html: Term by term: $B$ is the number of probes (a few hundred, grown over iterations); $u_b$ is a random unit direction; $\delta$ is a tiny probe radius; $\phi(x_t+\delta u_b)\in\{+1,-1\}$ is the single-query sign telling us which side that probe landed on; multiplying the sign by $u_b$ casts a vote; averaging over $B$ probes gives the estimated gradient direction. Intuitively, directions that point into the adversarial region accumulate positive votes, so the sum leans toward the boundary normal.

The deep reason this works — and the paper's key theoretical result — is that this estimator is asymptotically unbiased for the true gradient direction only when $x_t$ is exactly on the boundary. Estimate it from a point sitting well inside the adversarial region and the votes become lopsided (almost all probes land adversarial) and the estimate degrades. This single fact dictates the entire algorithm: it must keep returning to the boundary before every estimate — which is exactly what the 'hop back' step (two pages on) enforces.

The paper also debiases the estimate by subtracting the mean of the $\phi$ values, which sharpens accuracy when the probe outcomes are imbalanced. This is a small correction with an outsized effect on query efficiency.

With the gradient direction in hand, HSJA steps along it to cut the distance to the original image. But how big a step? Too big and you overshoot past the adversarial region (and waste the move); too small and you crawl. HSJA sets a principled base step length and then geometrically shrinks it — halving repeatedly — until the step lands somewhere still adversarial. Large steps early for fast progress, small steps late for fine refinement, all automatic.

Term by term: $\xi_t$ is the base step length at iteration $t$; $\lVert x_t - x_0\rVert_2$ is how far we still are from the original image $x_0$; dividing by $\sqrt{t}$ makes the step decay over time. Two behaviors fall out for free: the step is proportional to remaining distance, so it is bold when far and gentle when close; and the $1/\sqrt{t}$ decay gives the classic diminishing-step schedule that guarantees convergence. No hand-tuned constants — the schedule is derived, not guessed.

If a proposed jump of size $\xi_t$ lands on the wrong side, HSJA replaces $\xi_t$ with $\xi_t/2$, then $\xi_t/4$, and so on (the geometric progression), until a single label query confirms the new point is adversarial. This guarantees every jump makes real progress while spending only a handful of queries to size it.

After the jump, the point has moved into the adversarial interior — it is no longer on the boundary. But remember the iron rule from the gradient step: the Monte-Carlo estimate is only unbiased on the boundary. So before the next estimate, HSJA does a binary search along the straight line between the moved point and the original image, snapping back to the boundary surface where $S=0$. This is the move that earns the method its rhythm.

items: Hop — Monte-Carlo estimate of the gradient direction at the current boundary point (the only place it is unbiased).
Jump — step along that direction with a geometrically sized, decaying length to reduce distance to the original.
Land back — binary search along the line to the original to return precisely to the boundary, ready for the next hop.

blocks.html: Worked picture: you are on the boundary at distance 5.0 from the original. You estimate the gradient direction (hop), then jump along it; you overshoot to distance 3.5 but now sit inside the adversarial region. Binary search between distance-3.5 and the original finds the boundary at, say, distance 3.8 — closer than 5.0, and back on the surface. Repeat. Each loop ratchets the perturbation down.
Always estimate the gradient exactly on the boundary, because that is the only place the sign-based estimator is unbiased; the binary search exists to keep returning you there.

pages.title: State-of-the-art query efficiency
pages.subtitle: HSJA versus Boundary Attack and OPT

blocks.html: HopSkipJump reaches comparable or smaller perturbations with substantially fewer queries than the Boundary Attack and OPT — often an order of magnitude fewer in the low-query regime — across MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, in both $\ell_2$ and $\ell_\infty$ norms, for untargeted and targeted attacks. The gains come from two sources: spending queries on an asymptotically unbiased gradient direction instead of a blind random walk, and the principled geometric step schedule that needs no tuning.

The authors also pit HSJA against several defenses — defensive distillation, region-based classification, and adversarial training — and show it remains effective, making it a strong tool for honestly evaluating robustness. An attacker that needs only labels is very hard to defend against by hiding internals.

pages.title: Why this paper mattered
pages.subtitle: Closing the gap to white-box attacks

blocks.html: HopSkipJump pushed hard-label attacks to a level of query efficiency that turned them into a practical, standard benchmark for robustness evaluation rather than a worst-case curiosity. Its theoretical backbone — an asymptotically unbiased boundary gradient-direction estimator with an accompanying convergence analysis — gave the previously heuristic geometric intuition a firm mathematical footing. The author list (Jianbo Chen, Michael I. Jordan, Martin Wainwright) signals how much the statistics community engaged with adversarial robustness.

Seen against its siblings, the family forms a clean progression toward extracting maximum information per label query: the Boundary Attack random-walks the boundary (1 bit/query); OPT optimizes a direction by binary-search distance; Sign-OPT cheapens that with one-bit sign tests; HopSkipJump estimates the full gradient direction directly at the boundary and pairs it with geometric step sizing. Each step squeezes more signal from the same impoverished oracle.

A common misconception it helped retire: that adversarial training or output obfuscation makes a model safe in deployment. Because HSJA needs only labels and estimates gradients empirically, defenses that merely break or hide gradients (gradient masking) do little — echoing the lesson of the Obfuscated Gradients line of work.

HopSkipJump: Monte-Carlo gradient-direction estimation at the boundary, plus geometric step sizing and binary-search re-projection — yielding state-of-the-art query efficiency in the hard-label setting.
